mainTopic: A buyer's tithing obligation, when produce becomes obligated in מעשרות, and the sources for a worker and an ox eating attached and detached produce
overview: The amud opens by finishing the reading of the people of בית הינו, who said a seller or buyer does not have to tithe. The גמרא concludes that a buyer's obligation is only מדרבנן, with the פסוק as an אסמכתא. So the word כנפשך gets a new job: an employer who stops a worker from eating is not liable for muzzling, just like an owner who does not eat his own crop. Next, מר זוטרא challenges the rule that produce becomes obligated in tithes only in the house. He brings a משנה about cucumbers and gourds and a ברייתא about 'bringing in,' and the גמרא answers both. Then the גמרא goes back to a worker's right to eat. It asks for the source that a person may eat detached produce and that an ox may eat attached produce. Each time a קל וחומר is tried and rejected. The sources become the doubled words קמה and רעך, and רבי אמי offers a different reading from the vineyard פסוק. The amud ends with רבינא saying neither case needs its own פסוק, because both come from 'לא תחסם שור בדישו.' The explanation of how that works comes on the next amud.

steps.title: The verses בית הינו relied on
steps.stepSummary: The people of בית הינו read the פסוקים to mean that only the one who grows and eats produce must tithe it, not a seller or a buyer.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'You shall surely tithe… and you shall eat': but not one who sells. 'The produce of your seed': but not one who buys.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting how the people of בית הינו read the פסוקים about tithing to free sellers and buyers from the obligation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'eat' points to the eater, so a seller is left out. 'Your seed' points to the one who planted, so a buyer is left out. This reading sets up the question of whether a buyer must tithe by Torah law.

phrases.english: 'You shall surely tithe… and you shall eat':
but not one who sells.
'The produce of your seed':
but not one who buys.

steps.raayaObject: That a buyer is not obligated in tithes by Torah law
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 14:22–23, read through the words 'and you shall eat' and 'your seed'

steps.title: A buyer's tithing obligation is rabbinic
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that a buyer must tithe only by rabbinic law, and the פסוק is just a support.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the buyer's obligation is from the Rabbis, and the verse is merely a support.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts that by Torah law a buyer does not have to tithe. The obligation comes from the Rabbis, who attached it to the פסוק as a hint.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reading of בית הינו is correct as far as Torah law goes. Their mistake was ignoring the rabbinic obligation. An אסמכתא is a פסוק used as a hook for a rabbinic law, not as its real source.

keyTerms.meaning: A פסוק used only as a support or hint for a rabbinic law

steps.confusionAlert: Calling the obligation 'rabbinic' does not mean a buyer may skip tithing. It only means the Torah itself does not require it; the Rabbis do.
steps.whyThisMatters: If a buyer is exempt by Torah law, a worker surely is too. That means כנפשך is not needed to teach a worker's exemption, which leads straight into the next question.

phrases.english: Rather, it is from the Rabbis,
and the verse is merely a support.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides what level of law the derivation in step 1 reflects
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A buyer's duty to tithe is מדרבנן; the פסוק is only an אסמכתא.

steps.title: So what does כנפשך teach?
steps.stepSummary: Since a worker's exemption from tithing no longer needs the word כנפשך, the גמרא asks what that word comes to teach.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, what does 'like yourself' come to teach?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the word כנפשך is for, now that it is not needed to free a worker from tithing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, כנפשך was used to show that a worker may eat without tithing. If even a buyer is exempt by Torah law, a worker certainly is, so that reading is no longer needed. Every word in the Torah should teach something, so the גמרא looks for a new lesson.

keyTerms.meaning: Like yourself (from the פסוק about a worker eating in a vineyard)
What does it come to teach?

phrases.english: But then, what does 'like yourself' come to teach?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 2 took away the old job of כנפשך, so the גמרא asks for a new one
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What lesson the word כנפשך teaches

steps.title: כנפשך: no muzzling penalty for a worker
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that just as an owner who does not eat his own crop is not guilty of muzzling, an employer who stops a worker from eating is also exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: As taught in a ברייתא: 'Like yourself.' Just as with yourself, if you 'muzzled' yourself you are exempt, so too with a worker, if you muzzled him you are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא. כנפשך compares the worker to the owner: neither one being kept from eating creates guilt for muzzling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An owner who refuses to eat his own produce obviously does not break לא תחסום. The word כנפשך puts the worker in the same group. So an employer who stops a worker from eating is not punished under the muzzling prohibition.

keyTerms.meaning: As was taught in a ברייתא
You muzzled (did not let him eat)

steps.whatToRemember: כנפשך compares the worker to the owner: stopping a worker from eating does not make one liable for muzzling, just as an owner who does not eat is not liable.

phrases.english: For that which was taught in a baraita:
'Like yourself':
just as with yourself, if you muzzled, you are exempt,
phrases.notes: Here 'muzzled' means not eating. The exemption is from the prohibition of muzzling an ox while it threshes.

phrases.english: so too a worker, if you muzzled him, you are exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: כנפשך teaches that an employer who prevents a worker from eating is exempt from the muzzling prohibition, just like an owner who does not eat.

steps.title: מר זוטרא's challenge from cucumbers and gourds
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא cites a משנה saying cucumbers and gourds become obligated in tithes once they lose their blossom. That seems to happen even in the field, before they reach the house.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא objected: What is the 'threshing floor' point for tithes? For cucumbers and gourds, it is when they lose their blossom, and רבי אסי explained: when their blossom is removed. Doesn't this mean even in the field?
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא challenges the earlier rule that produce becomes obligated in tithes only once it reaches the house or courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה ties the obligation to the moment the blossom comes off, and says nothing about a house. If that can happen in the field, then the obligation can start before the produce sees the house or courtyard. That contradicts the earlier opinions.

keyTerms.meaning: Their 'threshing floor' for tithes: the point when tithing becomes required
The blossom or fuzz at the tip of the fruit

phrases.english: Mar Zutra objected:
What is their 'threshing floor' for tithes?
For cucumbers and gourds: from when they lose their blossom.
And Rabbi Asi said:
from when their blossom is removed.
Is it not that 'from when they lose their blossom'
applies even in the field!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the כנפשך topic and goes back to the earlier discussion of when produce becomes obligated in tithes
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that produce becomes obligated in tithes only once it sees the house or courtyard
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה links the obligation only to the blossom coming off, which can happen in the field, so the obligation would start before the house or courtyard

steps.title: The משנה means: in the house
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה refers to produce that loses its blossom in the house.
steps.simpleTranslation: No: it means from when they lose their blossom in the house.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the earlier rule by reading the משנה as talking about produce already in the house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Losing the blossom does not create the obligation alone. The house is still needed, and it obligates the produce only once the blossom is off. So the משנה adds a requirement rather than replacing the house.

phrases.english: No: from when they lose their blossom in the house.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers מר זוטרא's challenge
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case of the משנה to produce in the house
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה means the obligation starts once the blossom falls off, even in the field
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה means produce in the house becomes obligated once its blossom is off

steps.title: The wording should then be 'until'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the answer: if the house is the key, the משנה should have said 'until they lose their blossom,' not 'from when.'
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, instead of 'from when they lose their blossom,' it should have said 'until they lose their blossom'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 6 from the exact wording of the משנה. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'From when' sounds like the obligation starts the moment the blossom comes off, wherever the produce is. 'Until' would mean the obligation waits for the blossom to come off even when other conditions, like being in the house, are already met. Since the משנה said 'from when,' the reading of step 6 seems not to fit.

phrases.english: If so, why 'from when they lose their blossom'?
It should have said 'until they lose their blossom'!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי מִשֶּׁיְּפַקֵּסוּ עַד שֶׁיְּפַקֵּסוּ מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 6 from the wording of the משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the משנה refers to produce losing its blossom in the house
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'From when' suggests the obligation begins right away, wherever the produce is. If the house were required, the משנה should have said 'until.'

steps.title: Why the משנה says 'from when' and not 'until'
steps.stepSummary: Had the משנה said 'until,' we would think the produce is obligated only after the blossom loss is finished. 'From when' teaches that the obligation starts as soon as the blossom loss begins.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the משנה had said 'until they lose their blossom,' I would have thought it means until all of it has finished losing its blossom. So it tells us 'from when they lose their blossom,' meaning from the moment the blossom loss starts.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question about the wording of the משנה. The word 'from' shows exactly when the obligation starts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was that if the house is the real trigger, the משנה should have said 'until.' The answer is that 'until' could be misread as 'until the blossom loss is complete.' The word 'from' pins the moment to the beginning of the blossom loss, so the house-based answer still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: lose their blossom (the flower drops off the young fruit)
it teaches us (tells us something we would not have known)

phrases.english: If it had taught 'until they lose their blossom'
I would have said: until their blossom loss is complete,
so it teaches us: 'from when they lose their blossom,'
meaning from when their blossom loss begins.
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some have the word in square brackets. Both mean 'begins.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי תְּנָא עַד שֶׁיְּפַקֵּסוּ הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question in step 7
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why the wording was chosen: it avoids a mistaken reading
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Until' would mean only after the blossom loss is fully finished
steps.terutzMaskana: 'From' marks the start of the blossom loss, so the answer that the house matters stays in place

steps.title: מר זוטרא's ברייתא: produce is obligated once it is brought in
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says produce becomes טבל once its work is completed, meaning once it is brought in. That seems to include gathering it in the field.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא, son of רב נחמן, objected: The 'granary' point for tithes, which makes a person liable for eating טבל, is when the produce's work is completed. And what counts as completing its work? The work of bringing it in. Doesn't 'bringing it in' include bringing it in even while it is still in the field?
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge comes from a ברייתא. It seems to show that produce can become obligated in מעשר while it is still in the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier view was that produce becomes obligated only when it is brought into the house. The ברייתא says the trigger is 'bringing it in,' which could mean gathering it into a pile in the field. If so, produce becomes obligated before it ever reaches the house.

keyTerms.meaning: its 'granary' for tithes: the point when it becomes obligated
produce from which tithes have not yet been taken, and which may not be eaten

phrases.aramaic: מֵתִיב מָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra, son of Rav Naḥman, objected:
Its 'granary' for tithes,
phrases.notes: Here 'granary' means the moment the produce becomes obligated in tithes, not a building.

phrases.english: which makes one liable for it as untithed produce,
is from when their work is completed.
And what is the completion of their work?
The work of bringing them in.
Is it not bringing them in, even in the field?

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתִיב מָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge against the idea that the house is what obligates produce
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that produce becomes obligated in מעשר only when it is brought into the house
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא makes 'bringing in' the trigger, and this seems to include gathering in the field, before the house

steps.title: 'Bringing in' means bringing into the house
steps.stepSummary: No, the ברייתא means bringing the produce into the house. That is the completion of its work.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Bringing it into the house is what counts as completing its work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the reading of the ברייתא. 'Bringing in' means into the house, not into a pile in the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge depended on reading 'bringing in' broadly. The גמרא reads it narrowly as bringing into the house, so the ברייתא now agrees with the house-based view.

phrases.english: No, bringing them into the house,
that is the completion of their work.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers מר זוטרא's challenge by reading the ברייתא differently
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Bringing in' includes gathering in the field

steps.title: רבי ינאי's house rule applies only to olives and grapes
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: רבי ינאי's rule about the house was said only about olives and grapes, which do not have a granary. Wheat and barley become obligated at the granary, because the תורה explicitly says 'granary' about them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you want, say this: When רבי ינאי spoke, he meant olives and grapes, which are not 'granary' produce. But for wheat and barley, the word 'granary' is written explicitly about them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer. This time it accepts that the ברייתא may mean the field, and it narrows the earlier rule instead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of reinterpreting the ברייתא, this answer limits רבי ינאי's house rule to fruits like olives and grapes. Grain becomes obligated at the גורן in the field because a פסוק says so. So a ברייתא about grain does not contradict רבי ינאי.

keyTerms.meaning: and if you want, say (introduces a second answer)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways out. Either 'bringing in' means into the house, or the house rule covers only olives and grapes, while grain becomes obligated at the גורן.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
when Rabbi Yannai said his rule,
it was about olives and grapes,
which are not granary produce.
But wheat and barley,
'granary' is written explicitly about them.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא כִּי קָאָמַר רַבִּי יַנַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to מר זוטרא's challenge, given in place of step 10
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of the earlier rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי ינאי's house rule covers all produce
steps.terutzMaskana: The house rule covers only olives and grapes; grain is obligated at the גורן because the פסוק says so

steps.title: Source for a person eating from detached produce
steps.stepSummary: We have a source that a person may eat from attached produce and that an ox may eat from detached produce. Where do we learn that a person may eat from detached produce?
steps.simpleTranslation: We have found that a person may eat from attached produce, and that an ox may eat from detached produce. From where do we know that a person may eat from detached produce?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the worker's right to eat and asks for a missing source. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוקים gave us two cases: a person working attached produce, and an ox threshing detached produce. The case of a person working with detached produce has no source yet, so the גמרא asks for one.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. 'Attached' means still growing in the ground. 'Detached' means already cut, like grain being threshed.

phrases.english: We have found a person eating from attached produce
and an ox eating from detached produce.
phrases.notes: The ox comes from 'Do not muzzle an ox while it threshes,' דברים 25:4.

phrases.english: A person eating from detached produce, from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the tithes discussion and goes back to the source for a worker's right to eat
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק showing that a person may eat from detached produce while working

steps.title: First attempt: a קל וחומר from an ox
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to learn that a person may eat from detached produce through a קל וחומר from an ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: We can learn it from an ox. An ox may not eat from attached produce, yet it may eat from detached produce. A person may eat from attached produce, so surely he may eat from detached produce too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a first answer to the question from Step 12, using a קל וחומר (a logical 'how much more so' argument) from an ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox gets less: it may not eat from attached (מחובר) produce, yet it may eat from detached (תלוש) produce. A person gets more, since he may eat from attached produce. So the argument says he should surely also be allowed to eat from detached produce.

keyTerms.meaning: A 'how much more so' argument: if the weaker case has a rule, the stronger case surely has it too
Attached: produce still growing in the ground
Is it not logical? This is the closing line of a קל וחומר

phrases.english: It is learned by an a fortiori argument from an ox:
If an ox, which does not eat from attached produce,
still eats from detached produce,
then a person, who does eat from attached produce,
is it not logical that he eats from detached produce?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 12 with a קל וחומר.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A person may eat detached produce, learned by a קל וחומר from an ox, which may eat detached produce even though it may not eat attached produce.

steps.title: The ox has a special stringency: the ban on muzzling
steps.stepSummary: The קל וחומר is rejected because the ox has something special, the prohibition of muzzling, which does not apply to a person.
steps.simpleTranslation: But an ox is special, because you are commanded not to muzzle it. A person is not like that, because you are not commanded about muzzling him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the קל וחומר by showing that the ox has a special feature the person lacks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קל וחומר only works if the 'weaker' case is truly weaker in every way. Here the ox has its own extra protection, the ban on muzzling (חסימה). That may be why an ox may eat detached produce, and this reason does not carry over to a person.

keyTerms.meaning: What about...? It is special in that... This formula is used to break a קל וחומר
Muzzling: stopping an animal from eating while it works

phrases.english: What about an ox?
It is special, since you are commanded about muzzling it.
Can you say the same about a person,
whom you are not commanded about muzzling!

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה לְשׁוֹר שֶׁכֵּן אַתָּה מְצֻוֶּוה עַל חֲסִימָתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the קל וחומר of Step 13.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole קל וחומר from an ox.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ox has its own stringency, the ban on muzzling, that a person does not have, so the ox is not weaker in every way.

steps.title: Why not forbid muzzling a person too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the claim that there is no ban on muzzling a person, using its own קל וחומר from an ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let there be a command not to muzzle a person, learned from an ox. You are not commanded to keep an ox alive, yet you may not muzzle it. You are commanded to keep a person alive, so surely you may not muzzle him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the reason given in Step 14 by building a new קל וחומר to show that muzzling a person should also be forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If muzzling a person were forbidden too, the difference between ox and person would disappear and the first קל וחומר would work again. The argument: we have a greater duty to keep a person alive than an ox, so the ban on muzzling should surely apply to a person as well.

keyTerms.meaning: But let it be: a proposal that the rule should apply here too
To keep him alive, to support him

phrases.english: But let one be commanded about muzzling a person,
by an a fortiori argument from an ox:

phrases.aramaic: וּמָה שׁוֹר שֶׁאִי אַתָּה מְצֻוֶּוה לְהַחְיוֹתוֹ,
phrases.english: If an ox, which you are not commanded to keep alive,
you are still commanded about muzzling it,
then a person, whom you are commanded to keep alive,

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ דִּין שֶׁאַתָּה מְצֻוֶּוה עַל חֲסִימָתוֹ?!
phrases.english: is it not logical that you are commanded about muzzling him?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וִיהֵא אָדָם מְצֻוֶּוה עַל חֲסִימָתוֹ מִקַּל וָחוֹמֶר מִשּׁוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason used in Step 14 to reject the קל וחומר.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 14 that there is no command about muzzling a person.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר: the duty to keep a person alive is greater than for an ox, so the ban on muzzling should apply to a person even more.

steps.title: כנפשך: a worker is treated like the owner himself
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says כנפשך, teaching that a worker is like the owner himself. Since one is not punished for muzzling himself, one is not punished for muzzling a worker.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'like yourself.' The worker is treated like your own self. Just as you are not punished if you muzzle yourself, you are not punished if you muzzle the worker.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends Step 14 by bringing a פסוק showing that muzzling a person is not punishable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קל וחומר cannot override what a פסוק teaches. The word כנפשך puts the פועל in the same category as the owner, and nobody is punished for 'muzzling' himself. So the difference between ox and person stands, and the first קל וחומר remains broken.

keyTerms.meaning: Like yourself: a word from the פסוק about a worker eating grapes

phrases.english: The verse says: "Like yourself,"
so the worker's self is like your own self:
just as with himself, if you muzzled him you are exempt,
phrases.notes: He means the owner himself: if he keeps himself from eating, there is no punishment.

phrases.english: so too a worker, if you muzzled him you are exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 15 with a פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A פסוק overrides the קל וחומר.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Muzzling a worker should be forbidden, just like muzzling an ox.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because of כנפשך, a worker is like the owner himself, and one is not punished for muzzling him.
steps.confusionAlert: The point is not that it is fine to stop a worker from eating. The גמרא only says one is not punished under the ox's prohibition of muzzling.

steps.title: So where do we learn detached produce for a person?
steps.stepSummary: Since the קל וחומר failed, the גמרא asks again for the source that a person may eat from detached produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, how do we know that a person may eat from detached produce?
steps.whatsHappening: After the first answer fell apart, the גמרא goes back to the original question from Step 12. This line sets up the real answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 13–16 ended with the קל וחומר still rejected. So the question of Step 12 is open again and needs a different source.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, if so: used when an earlier answer has failed
From where do we know it?

phrases.english: Rather, from where do we learn that a person may eat from detached produce?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Since the קל וחומר of Step 13 stayed rejected, the question of Step 12 is asked again.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source in the תורה that a worker may eat from detached produce.

steps.title: The doubled word קמה teaches detached produce
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says קמה twice. One mention teaches attached produce, so the extra one teaches detached produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'standing grain' two times. If the second one is not needed for a person eating attached produce, use it for a person eating detached produce.
steps.whatsHappening: After the קל וחומר failed, the גמרא answers the question of step 17: the source is the extra word קמה in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first קמה already teaches that a worker may eat from attached (מחובר) produce. Since the תורה has no wasted words, the second קמה must teach something new, and it is applied to detached (תלוש) produce. This uses the rule 'אם אינו ענין': an extra word not needed for its own topic is moved to another topic.

keyTerms.meaning: If it is not needed for this topic, apply it to another topic: a way of reading an extra word

steps.whatToRemember: The קל וחומר from an ox fails, because only an ox has a ban on muzzling, and כנפשך shows muzzling a worker is not punishable. A worker's right to eat detached produce comes from the extra word קמה.

phrases.english: The verse says "standing grain," "standing grain,"
two times.
If it is not needed for a person eating attached produce,
apply it to a person eating detached produce.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר קְרָא קָמָה קָמָה שְׁתֵּי פְּעָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The repeated word קמה: the extra mention teaches that a person may eat from detached produce.
steps.whyThisMatters: It gives a firm source in the תורה for a worker's right to eat detached produce, after logic alone failed.

steps.title: רבי אמי: A person eating detached produce needs no extra verse
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי says the vineyard פסוק already covers a worker carrying picked grapes, so no separate source is needed for תלוש.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי said: We don't need a special verse to teach that a person may eat from detached produce. It is written, 'When you come into your neighbor's vineyard.' That verse must include even a worker hired to carry the grapes, and the תורה still says he may eat.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי gives a different answer to the question from Step 17. He says the regular vineyard פסוק already teaches that a worker may eat detached produce.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 18 needed the extra word קמה to teach תלוש. רבי אמי says that is not necessary. A worker hired to carry grapes is handling grapes that are already picked, and the פסוק still lets him eat.

keyTerms.meaning: To carry on the shoulder, to haul
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

phrases.english: Rabbi Ami said:
A person with detached produce does not need a verse.
It is written: "When you come into your neighbor's vineyard"
Are we not dealing even with a case where he hired him to carry,
phrases.notes: If he's carrying grapes out of the vineyard, they're already picked, so this is detached produce.

phrases.english: and the Merciful One said he may eat.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אַמֵּי אָמַר: אָדָם בְּתָלוּשׁ לָא צְרִיךְ קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the question of Step 17, in place of the קמה derivation of Step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The vineyard פסוק already includes a worker hauling picked grapes, so תלוש for a person needs no extra source.

steps.title: Asking the source for an ox eating attached produce
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know an ox may eat from produce still attached to the ground.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know that an ox may eat from attached produce?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from the person to the ox and asks for the source. This sets up the next move, a קל וחומר attempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox's right to eat detached produce is clear, since the threshing case is about detached grain. What still needs a source is the ox eating produce that is still growing.

keyTerms.meaning: Attached produce, still growing in the ground
From where do we know it?

phrases.english: An ox with attached produce, from where do we know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Having covered a person in both cases, turns to the ox in the attached case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that an ox may eat attached produce.

steps.title: A קל וחומר from a person to an ox
steps.stepSummary: If a person, who has no explicit right to detached produce, eats attached produce, then surely an ox, which does eat detached produce, eats attached produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learn it with a קל וחומר from a person. A person does not eat from detached produce, yet he eats from attached produce. An ox does eat from detached produce, so it should surely eat from attached produce too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a קל וחומר. It argues that the ox is 'stronger' than a person, so it should get what a person gets.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox has a clear right in detached produce, and the person has a clear right in attached produce. Since the ox seems to have the stronger right, the גמרא wants to give it the person's right to attached produce as well.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it not logical? The closing words of a קל וחומר

phrases.english: A קל וחומר from a person:
If a person, who does not eat from detached produce,
phrases.notes: He means there is no explicit verse for a person eating detached produce.

phrases.english: eats from attached produce,
then an ox, which eats from detached produce,
is it not logical that it eats from attached produce?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 20's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A קל וחומר from a person teaches that an ox eats attached produce.

steps.title: Rejected: we must keep a person alive, but not an ox
steps.stepSummary: A person is special because there is a command to sustain him, so his rights cannot be passed on to an ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is special about a person? You are commanded to keep him alive. Can you say the same about an ox, which you are not commanded to keep alive?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the קל וחומר. A person has a special feature that the ox lacks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קל וחומר fails if the starting case has an extra reason for its law. A person's right to eat may come from the command to sustain him, and that command does not apply to an ox.

keyTerms.meaning: What about...? The opening of a rejection that points out something special
To keep him alive, to sustain him

phrases.english: What is special about a person?
That you are commanded to keep him alive.
Will you say so about an ox,
which you are not commanded to keep alive!

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה לְאָדָם שֶׁכֵּן אַתָּה מְצֻוֶּוה לְהַחְיוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the קל וחומר of Step 21.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole קל וחומר from a person to an ox.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A person has the command to sustain him, which an ox lacks.

steps.title: Challenge: an ox should also be included in the command to sustain
steps.stepSummary: Using a new קל וחומר, the גמרא argues that an ox should be covered by the command to sustain, since its muzzling is forbidden while a person's is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us be commanded to keep an ox alive too, by a קל וחומר. A person may be muzzled without breaking a command, yet we must keep him alive. An ox may not be muzzled, so surely we must keep it alive.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back against the rejection. It tries to give the ox the same special feature the person has.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If an ox can also be included in the command to sustain, the difference from Step 22 disappears and the first קל וחומר works again. The argument uses the ban on חסימה from Steps 14-16, which applies to an ox and not to a person.

keyTerms.meaning: Muzzling, blocking an animal from eating while it works

phrases.english: But let one be commanded to keep an ox alive,
from a קל וחומר:

phrases.aramaic: וּמָה אָדָם שֶׁאִי אַתָּה מְצֻוֶּוה עַל חֲסִימָתוֹ
phrases.english: If a person, whose muzzling you are not commanded about,
is someone you are commanded to keep alive,
then an ox, whose muzzling you are commanded about,
is it not logical that you are commanded to keep it alive?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וִיהֵא שׁוֹר מְצֻוֶּוה לְהַחְיוֹתוֹ, מִקַּל וָחוֹמֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rejection in Step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 22 that an ox is not covered by the command to sustain.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Muzzling is forbidden for an ox but not for a person, so the ox's protection seems stronger and should include being sustained.

steps.title: The פסוק limits sustaining to 'your brother'
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'and your brother shall live with you' limits the command to a person, not an ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says, 'And your brother shall live with you.' Your brother, and not an ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with a פסוק. The command to sustain applies only to a fellow person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פסוק overrides a קל וחומר. The word אחיך shows that the command to keep someone alive is for people only, so the difference in Step 22 stands and the first קל וחומר still fails.

phrases.english: The verse says: "And your brother shall live with you,"
your brother, and not an ox.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Verse limits the scope of the law
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An ox should be covered by the command to sustain, because of a קל וחומר from muzzling.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק says אחיך, so only a person is covered, and the rejection of the first קל וחומר stands.

steps.title: So what is the source for an ox and attached produce?
steps.stepSummary: With the קל וחומר gone, the גמרא asks again for the source that an ox eats attached produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, from where do we know that an ox may eat from attached produce?
steps.whatsHappening: The קל וחומר has failed, so the גמרא goes back to its question from Step 20. This sets up the final answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is claimed here. The גמרא simply admits that logic did not work and that it needs a source from the text.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, then. It signals a fresh search after a failed attempt

phrases.english: Rather, an ox with attached produce, from where do we know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the question of Step 20 after the קל וחומר was rejected.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A new source that an ox eats attached produce.

steps.title: The double word רעך teaches about an ox
steps.stepSummary: רעך appears twice. One teaches a person with attached produce, and the extra one teaches an ox with attached produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says 'your neighbor,' 'your neighbor' twice. If the extra one is not needed for a person with attached produce, apply it to an ox with attached produce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finds the source in an extra word of the פסוק. The repeated word is used to teach the ox's right to attached produce.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only one רעך is needed for a person eating attached produce. The extra mention is not needed there, so the גמרא uses it for the ox. This follows the same method as the double קמה in Step 18.

keyTerms.meaning: If it is not needed for this matter

steps.whatToRemember: A person eats attached produce from the פסוק, and detached produce from either the double קמה or רבי אמי's reading. An ox eats attached produce from the double רעך, because the קל וחומר failed: only a person is covered by the command to sustain (אחיך ולא שור).

phrases.english: The verse says "your neighbor," "your neighbor" two times,
if it is not needed for a person with attached produce,
apply it to an ox with attached produce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 25's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra רעך teaches that an ox eats attached produce.

steps.title: רבינא: Two cases need no separate verses
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says no special פסוק is needed for a person eating detached produce or for an ox eating attached produce. He points to the verse 'You shall not muzzle an ox in its threshing.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: We do not need verses to teach that a person may eat from detached produce, or that an ox may eat from attached produce, because it is written: 'You shall not muzzle an ox in its threshing.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא offers a new approach. He says two of the cases the גמרא has been working on do not need their own פסוקים, and he points to the verse about not muzzling an ox. How that verse covers both cases is explained on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the גמרא looked for a separate source for each case, and in the last step it used the extra word רעך for an ox with attached produce. רבינא says this extra searching is not needed: the case of a person with detached produce and the case of an ox with attached produce can both come from the verse 'לא תחסם שור בדישו'. On this amud he only makes this claim and names the verse. How the verse covers both cases is explained on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: Detached produce, already cut off from the ground
Attached produce, still growing in the ground
Do not muzzle (do not block the animal's mouth)
Threshing, beating grain to separate the kernels

steps.confusionAlert: רבינא is not saying these two laws are not true. He agrees a person may eat detached produce and an ox may eat attached produce. He only says we do not need separate פסוקים to teach them.
steps.whyThisMatters: This changes how the whole search for sources works: one verse may cover cases the גמרא thought each needed its own source.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
Neither for a person with detached produce
nor for an ox with attached produce
are verses needed,
phrases.notes: He means these laws are still true. They just don't need their own separate verse.

phrases.english: as it is written: 'You shall not muzzle an ox in its threshing.'

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבִינָא אָמַר: לָא אָדָם בְּתָלוּשׁ וְלֹא שׁוֹר בִּמְחוּבָּר צְרִיכִי קְרָאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different approach to both the double-קמה derivation (step 18) and the double-רעך derivation (step 26), saying separate verses are not needed for these two cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person eating detached produce and an ox eating attached produce do not need their own verses. They come from 'לא תחסם שור בדישו'.
